At the block office in Kuttanad, the ceiling fan turned slowly over stacks of crop-loss forms. Anjali had been interning there for four months, and she no longer read the farmers' names before stamping.
Joseph, the other intern, came in with mud to his ankles. "Chechi from the east paddy says the new drainage is working! She wants us to come and see."
Anjali didn't look up. "Great. Another photo for a report nobody in the head office opens."
"You used to love the field visits."
"I used to think they mattered." She stamped another form.
Joseph stood there a moment, his excitement draining, then went back out.
At the tea shop later she laughed with the clerk about "Saint Joseph and his drains". Walking home along the canal, she felt nothing about any of it, and the nothing felt safer than caring.

qa.q: What had Anjali stopped doing before stamping the forms?
qa.a: She no longer read the farmers' names before stamping.

qa.q: Why might feeling 'nothing' seem safer to Anjali than caring?
qa.a: She is worn out after four months, and not caring protects her from the effort and disappointment that caring would cost.

qa.q: What turning point could help Anjali now?
qa.a: She could notice that the sneering is a sign of exhaustion, talk honestly with her supervisor about her workload, and get real rest instead of hiding behind jokes.

qa.q: What is it like for Joseph when Anjali brushes off the drainage news?
qa.a: Joseph arrives excited from the field and feels his excitement drain away 😔; if he heard the 'Saint Joseph' joke, he might feel mocked for caring.

grounding: Illustrates an intern who has come to see the work as pointless and sneers at a colleague who still cares, with detachment protecting a tired mind.

passage:
Karthik, you're rolling your eyes at your project. I know that look. Let me tell you something from my final year of engineering.
I was a girl of twenty-one then. By the last semester, I was so tired that everything seemed pointless. Projects? Pointless. Placements? A lottery. When my friend Radha stayed up to perfect her circuit, I said, "Why bother? Nobody reads these." I laughed at people who still cared. I thought I was being clever.
Later I understood. I wasn't clever. I was exhausted. Caring had become too expensive, so I stopped.
My professor noticed. She asked me, "Neelam, when did you last sleep properly?" That question cracked something open. So, Karthik, when you sneer, ask yourself that.

qa.q: What was Neelam's friend Radha doing?
qa.a: Staying up to perfect her circuit.

qa.q: What was young Neelam feeling when she laughed at people who cared?
qa.a: She felt exhausted and detached, protecting herself because caring had become too expensive.

qa.q: In the story, what turning point helped Neelam?
qa.a: Her professor asking when she last slept properly, which helped her see the cynicism was exhaustion.

qa.q: How might Radha have felt when Neelam said "Why bother?"
qa.a: Radha may have felt hurt and discouraged by her friend's sneer at work she cared about.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling her final-year cynicism, sneering at friends who cared, as an exhausted mind's protection.

Final-year project demos were in three days, the lab's air conditioner had broken, and Lalit hadn't slept more than four hours a night in weeks.
Chinmay was at the next bench, rewiring his drone for the fifth time. "Lalit, can you check my code?"
"Why? It's a college project. Nobody cares."
"I care."
"That's your problem." Lalit leaned back and closed his eyes. "We'll all end up in the same boring jobs anyway."
Chinmay's face fell.
Lalit felt a flicker of something like shame, and pushed it down. Caring took energy. He had none left. Easier to sneer.
He opened his own project folder. He hadn't touched it in a week.

qa.q: How many hours had Lalit been sleeping a night?
qa.a: No more than four hours.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling when he pushed down the flicker of shame?
qa.a: He felt ashamed for a moment but too exhausted to care, so he chose sneering as protection.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Lalit now?
qa.a: Admitting he is exhausted, getting proper sleep, and talking to a mentor or counsellor before the detachment grows.

qa.q: What is it like for Chinmay when Lalit says "That's your problem"?
qa.a: Chinmay feels hurt and deflated, his care mocked by a friend.

grounding: Shows a final-year student, exhausted, calling the work pointless and sneering at a classmate who still cares.

At the Gurugram consulting firm, the interns had a group chat. Sangeeta used to send the most messages: questions, ideas, late-night slides. Now she mostly sent eye-roll replies.
When Sachin posted, "Anyone want to practise the client pitch?", she wrote, "lol why. They'll ignore our slides anyway."
At lunch he asked her directly. "You used to love this. What happened?"
"I grew up," she said. "It's all pointless, Sachin. Busywork."
But walking back to her desk, she noticed she hadn't slept properly in a month. She felt heavy, not grown-up. Caring about the pitch felt like lifting something she couldn't lift any more.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta reply when Sachin asked about practising the pitch?
qa.a: "lol why. They'll ignore our slides anyway."

qa.q: What was Sangeeta feeling as she walked back to her desk?
qa.a: She felt heavy and exhausted, and the cynicism was covering how drained she was.

qa.q: What small step could help Sangeeta at this stage?
qa.a: Admitting to herself or Sachin that she's exhausted, resting properly, and talking to her supervisor about her load.

qa.q: What might Sachin be experiencing when Sangeeta says "It's all pointless"?
qa.a: Sachin seems puzzled and concerned, missing the eager Sangeeta he used to know.

grounding: Shows an intern who feels the work is pointless and mocks a colleague who still cares, cynicism covering exhaustion.

"You're still colour-coding the survey data?" Lokesh leaned back until his chair creaked. "Gautam, nobody reads final-year projects. The external will flip three pages and sign."
"I just want it to be decent," Gautam said, eyes on the screen.
"Decent." Lokesh laughed without smiling. "Last year I'd have stayed till midnight with you. Now I can't even open the file. What's the point?"
"You built half this model. You loved it in August."
"August me was an idiot. Look at them." He nodded at the next bench, where two classmates were arguing happily over a chart. "Acting like it matters."
Gautam turned from the screen. "You've been saying that about everything lately. The fest, placements, even cricket."
Lokesh rubbed his eyes. "I'm just tired, man. Tired of caring."
"Then maybe that's the thing to talk about. Not the project."

qa.q: What did Lokesh say the external examiner will do?
qa.a: Flip three pages and sign.

qa.q: What feelings might sit underneath Lokesh's sneering at the classmates?
qa.a: He is exhausted and tired of caring; mocking others protects him from caring about work he no longer has the energy for.

qa.q: What could Gautam suggest next?
qa.a: Gautam could gently ask how long Lokesh has felt this tired and suggest talking to a mentor or the college counsellor.

qa.q: How might Gautam feel watching his friend change?
qa.a: He seems concerned and a little hurt, remembering how much Lokesh loved the model in August.

grounding: Shows a final-year student calling the work pointless and sneering at classmates who care, a cynicism that shields an exhausted mind.
